narrative:
The model that reviewed your application estimates you have a 58.9 percent chance of failing the bar exam on the first attempt. This means that, based on the patterns seen in thousands of past students, failure is more likely than success, and it is this prediction that led to the denial of your application.

The single most influential factor in this prediction was your Law School Admission Test score. At 22.5, your score is drastically lower than the average of 37.2 among admitted students, and this gap was the dominant signal in the review. A score that low strongly suggests that you are not yet prepared for the academic demands of law school, and it pushed the prediction firmly toward bar exam failure.

Your undergraduate grade point average of 2.90 is below the 3.23 average for admitted students, but surprisingly, this factor did not hurt you. It actually nudged the prediction slightly in the direction of passing, suggesting that your overall college record is stronger than what the model typically sees from applicants with such a low test score. Your family income falling in the middle bracket also had a smaller, positive influence, similarly tilting the prediction toward success.

What should you do next? The clearest path forward is to retake the LSAT. Your grades show that you can handle demanding coursework, but the test score is the main obstacle standing between you and admission. Invest in intensive LSAT preparation and consider reapplying once you have raised your score substantially, as doing so would directly reverse the strongest reason your application was denied.
